title: When Two Mutants Rescue Each Other

scenes.tts: How can two pure-breeding white-eyed flies have red-eyed offspring? Watch their chromosome copies enter one shared cell. Each parent carries a different hidden loss. The offspring eye begins white, waiting to see whether normal function returns.
scenes.caption: How can two pure-breeding white-eyed flies have red-eyed offspring? Watch their chromosome copies enter one shared cell. Each parent carries a different hidden loss. The offspring eye begins white, waiting to see whether normal function returns.
scenes.visual: Hook first, no title card. Two large schematic white fly eyes fill the left and right thirds. A central offspring eye begins white. From each parent, one chromosome bar glides into a large outlined cell beneath the offspring. Keep particles moving slowly. COLOR MAP: gene A and its product blue; gene B and its product gold; observed rescue and wild type green; a tested break or failure red; inactive context gray. Mark all gene diagrams 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: How can two pure-breeding white-eyed flies have red-eyed offspring? Watch their chromosome copies enter one shared cell. Each parent carries a different hidden loss. The offspring eye begins white, waiting to see whether normal function returns.

scenes.tts: A red eye needs several genes working together. Some genes make pigments. Others move pigments into granules. A missing shared transporter leaves the eye white. So does blocking both pigment pathways. Appearance alone cannot tell which gene broke.
scenes.caption: A red eye needs several genes working together. Some genes make pigments. Others move pigments into granules. A missing shared transporter leaves the eye white. So does blocking both pigment pathways. Appearance alone cannot tell which gene broke.
scenes.visual: Transform the central eye into one carried schematic cell. Two gray pigment-making blocks, labelled 'red pigment' and 'brown pigment', both feed one gray block labelled 'shared transporter', which carries pigment into a granule and colors the eye red. First drop a red barrier on the transporter; the eye drains to white. Reset. Then drop red barriers on both pigment blocks together; the eye drains to white again. Never block only one pigment block. Keep the pathway spanning most of the frame and mark it 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: A red eye needs several genes working together. Some genes make pigments. Others move pigments into granules. A missing shared transporter leaves the eye white. So does blocking both pigment pathways. Appearance alone cannot tell which gene broke.

scenes.tts: An allele is one version of a gene. A diploid cell carries paired chromosome copies, so it can carry paired alleles. For a recessive loss, one working allele usually makes enough product. That product works at its normal place in the cell.
scenes.caption: An allele is one version of a gene. A diploid cell carries paired chromosome copies, so it can carry paired alleles. For a recessive loss, one working allele usually makes enough product. That product works at its normal place in the cell.
scenes.visual: Keep the shared cell. Enlarge one blue gene block on each homologous chromosome and label each version 'allele'. Then pull back to show the paired chromosomes inside one diploid cell. Blue product from the one working allele gathers at its own fixed site in the cell and lights it fully, labelled 'enough from one copy'. Do not show product spreading through the cytoplasm.
scenes.narration: An allele is one version of a gene. A diploid cell carries paired chromosome copies, so it can carry paired alleles. For a recessive loss, one working allele usually makes enough product. That product works at its normal place in the cell.

scenes.tts: First check each mutation against wild type. If a working copy restores the ordinary phenotype, the mutation is recessive. That check matters because complementation reads rescue. A dominant mutation can keep the cell mutant beside any partner.
scenes.caption: First check each mutation against wild type. If a working copy restores the ordinary phenotype, the mutation is recessive. That check matters because complementation reads rescue. A dominant mutation can keep the cell mutant beside any partner.
scenes.visual: Carry the cell forward. Pair one red-broken blue gene block with a green-outlined working blue copy. The eye fills red and a label 'recessive' settles. Briefly replace the broken copy with a red dominant-effect badge; the eye remains white and the readout becomes 'test uninformative'. Do not label it same gene.
scenes.narration: First check each mutation against wild type. If a working copy restores the ordinary phenotype, the mutation is recessive. That check matters because complementation reads rescue. A dominant mutation can keep the cell mutant beside any partner.

scenes.tts: Now combine the checked recessive mutations on opposite chromosome copies in one diploid cell. This arrangement is trans. One chromosome has broken gene A and working gene B. The other has working A and broken B.
scenes.caption: Now combine the checked recessive mutations on opposite chromosome copies in one diploid cell. This arrangement is trans. One chromosome has broken gene A and working gene B. The other has working A and broken B.
scenes.visual: Two homologous chromosome bars enlarge and align vertically inside the same cell. On the upper bar, blue A is crossed in red and gold B glows. On the lower, blue A glows and gold B is crossed. Animate the word 'trans' between opposite bars. The eye readout stays unresolved.
scenes.narration: Now combine the checked recessive mutations on opposite chromosome copies in one diploid cell. This arrangement is trans. One chromosome has broken gene A and working gene B. The other has working A and broken B.

scenes.tts: Will this cell recover its red eye, or stay white? Follow the working copies, not the broken ones. Decide whether the shared cell now has every function it needs.
scenes.caption: Will this cell recover its red eye, or stay white? Follow the working copies, not the broken ones. Decide whether the shared cell now has every function it needs.
scenes.visual: Keep both chromosome bars large. Pulse the working blue A and working gold B gently, but do not draw products or reveal the eye. Center the question 'Recover or stay white?' above the unresolved white eye. Ambient motion continues.
scenes.narration: Will this cell recover its red eye, or stay white? Follow the working copies, not the broken ones. Decide whether the shared cell now has every function it needs.

scenes.visual: Hold the unresolved question and chromosome pair for thinking. Working blue A and gold B continue a slow pulse; the white eye and question remain unchanged.

scenes.tts: The working A copy supplies the blue function. The working B copy supplies the gold function. With both functions present in the cell, red pigment appears. Normal function returns, so the mutations complement.
scenes.caption: The working A copy supplies the blue function. The working B copy supplies the gold function. With both functions present in the cell, red pigment appears. Normal function returns, so the mutations complement.
scenes.visual: A blue function token lights the matching blue block in the carried pathway; a gold token lights the matching gold block. Each token stays at its own block. Green flow crosses the entire path, the central eye fills red, and a green 'complement' label grows beneath it.
scenes.narration: The working A copy supplies the blue function. The working B copy supplies the gold function. With both functions present in the cell, red pigment appears. Normal function returns, so the mutations complement.

scenes.tts: Reset the cell. Now both chromosomes carry broken alleles of gene A, while gene B works. No working A product appears. The eye stays white, so these mutations fail to complement under the simple model.
scenes.caption: Reset the cell. Now both chromosomes carry broken alleles of gene A, while gene B works. No working A product appears. The eye stays white, so these mutations fail to complement under the simple model.
scenes.visual: Clear the previous green answer before changing the case. Both blue A blocks gain red breaks; both gold B blocks glow. Gold tokens reach their block, but the blue block remains dark. The pathway stops, the eye stays white, and 'fail to complement' appears in red.
scenes.narration: Reset the cell. Now both chromosomes carry broken alleles of gene A, while gene B works. No working A product appears. The eye stays white, so these mutations fail to complement under the simple model.

scenes.tts: Mutations that fail with one another form a complementation group. In the simple model, a group usually marks one gene. Testing many pairs turns one shared phenotype into groups, revealing how many functions the screen happened to hit.
scenes.caption: Mutations that fail with one another form a complementation group. In the simple model, a group usually marks one gene. Testing many pairs turns one shared phenotype into groups, revealing how many functions the screen happened to hit.
scenes.visual: Transform the chromosome pair into a schematic grid of unlabeled mutant dots. Pairwise tests sweep across it. Red failure links gather some dots into a blue-outlined group and others into a gold-outlined group; green complement links fade after sorting. End with 'at least this many genes', without a number.
scenes.narration: Mutations that fail with one another form a complementation group. In the simple model, a group usually marks one gene. Testing many pairs turns one shared phenotype into groups, revealing how many functions the screen happened to hit.

scenes.tts: The rule has boundaries. Intragenic complementation can rescue different alleles of one gene. Mutations in different genes can sometimes fail together. Those exceptions refine the test. They do not change what a clean recessive result usually means.
scenes.caption: The rule has boundaries. Intragenic complementation can rescue different alleles of one gene. Mutations in different genes can sometimes fail together. Those exceptions refine the test. They do not change what a clean recessive result usually means.
scenes.visual: Return to the shared cell. The ordinary different-gene rescue occupies the large center panel. Two smaller edge cards appear, both marked 'exception': 'same gene may rescue' and 'different genes may fail'. Keep them subordinate and schematic. The center panel remains labelled 'usual simple result'.
scenes.narration: The rule has boundaries. Intragenic complementation can rescue different alleles of one gene. Mutations in different genes can sometimes fail together. Those exceptions refine the test. They do not change what a clean recessive result usually means.

scenes.tts: Always name what the test measured. A red eye is observed rescue, not direct proof of chromosome position. Mapping asks where mutations sit. Complementation asks whether their functions can supply each other in one cell.
scenes.caption: Always name what the test measured. A red eye is observed rescue, not direct proof of chromosome position. Mapping asks where mutations sit. Complementation asks whether their functions can supply each other in one cell.
scenes.visual: Split the frame without changing the color map. On the left, the red eye and green rescue label stay under 'function'. On the right, gray chromosome tick marks sit under 'position'. A moving divider keeps the questions separate; highlight only the function side as the film's readout.
scenes.narration: Always name what the test measured. A red eye is observed rescue, not direct proof of chromosome position. Mapping asks where mutations sit. Complementation asks whether their functions can supply each other in one cell.

scenes.visual: End card, one line only: 'For recessive mutants, rescue in trans usually means different genes.' Center the line in large type. No title, subtitle, logo, or smaller line.
